summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, SVC syndrome, and multiple prior surgeries was admitted with a Crohn’s flare, abdominal pain, and facial swelling. Imaging showed no bowel obstruction but revealed chronic complete occlusion of the SVC and brachiocephalic veins with collateralization, explaining her neck swelling. She developed a suspected central line infection in her right internal jugular catheter, presenting with fever and erythema, and was treated with intravenous Vancomycin. Due to non-functional lines and venous thrombosis, she required multiple central line revisions, ultimately receiving a femoral tunneled line for outpatient antibiotic therapy, which dislodged before discharge. Her abdominal symptoms improved with bowel rest, NG decompression, and pain management. She was discharged home after nine days of antibiotics, afebrile, with improved pain control, and a plan for close outpatient follow-up, including blood work and monitoring for infection recurrence.
